subject: botany
question_text: List three strategies that a bisexual chasmogamous flower can evolve to prevent self-pollination.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section (book p.18, SAQ 1). Botany holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The book prints 'to present self pollination' (scan error for 'prevent') and 'Primula-diheterostyly' (mangling of distyly); both are cleaned here.

page_header: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants · 4 marks

steps.label: The three strategies
lines: These three prevent self-pollination in a
steps.why: The question says 'list three', so the examiner first looks for the three names together — box them before explaining each one.
common_mistakes: Writing self-incompatibility or unisexuality here. Those stop selfing too, but this list is for a BISEXUAL open flower.
Explaining one strategy at length and never naming the other two.
steps.memory_tip: Time, height, style-length: organs mature at different TIMES, sit at different HEIGHTS, styles have different LENGTHS.
steps.margin_note: One boxed line with all three names — the listing mark is separate from the explanations.

steps.label: Dichogamy
lines: Dichogamy: the male and female sex organs of
the flower mature at different times.
Protandry: anthers mature first. Eg: sunflower
Protogyny: stigma matures first. Eg: Solanum
steps.why: If pollen is shed when the stigma of the same flower is not receptive, self-pollination cannot happen — a timing separation, in two directions with a name each.
common_mistakes: Swapping protandry and protogyny. Andro = male first, gyno = female first.
Leaving out the two sub-types — they carry the detail this mark pays for.
steps.memory_tip: ProtANDRY = ANDRoecium (male) early; protoGYNY = GYNoecium (female) early.
steps.margin_note: Definition plus both sub-types with one example each — four short lines.

steps.label: Herkogamy
lines: Herkogamy: the anthers and the stigma are
placed at different heights (eg: Hibiscus) or
steps.why: Here the separation is in SPACE: with a physical gap or a direction mismatch between anther and stigma, pollen from the same flower does not reach its own stigma.
common_mistakes: Confusing herkogamy with heterostyly — herkogamy is within ONE flower's geometry; heterostyly compares flowers of the same species.
Giving no example. Hibiscus is the standard one.
steps.memory_tip: Herkogamy = a hurdle in space: same flower, organs kept apart.
steps.margin_note: Two placements (height, direction) with an example each is the full point.

steps.label: Heterostyly
lines: Heterostyly: flowers of the same species have
styles of different lengths, so anther and
stigma never sit at the same level.
steps.why: Long-styled and short-styled flowers on different plants match anther height to a DIFFERENT flower's stigma height, so pollen transfer works between morphs, not within one flower.
common_mistakes: Writing 'different styles in the same flower' — the different lengths are across flowers of the species.
Missing the example. Primula is the textbook case.
steps.memory_tip: Hetero-STYLY: the STYLE length varies across the species — pin and thrum flowers of Primula.
steps.margin_note: The book's 'di-heterostyly' means distyly — two style-length forms in Primula.

insider_note: The four marks here are 1 for the list and 1 per explanation — a beautifully written essay on dichogamy alone still scores 2 at most.
